Give events stable identifiers, deduplicate processing, and use version checks or event sequence information when the source provides it. Make transitions conditional on current state rather than arrival order alone. Reconcile against the source of truth when ordering is uncertain. Record ignored duplicates so operators can explain unexpected delivery patterns.

Define the schedule, timezone, overlap policy, authorization scope, and a budget per run. Use stable run identifiers and prevent unintended concurrent executions. Handle daylight-saving changes, missed schedules, and retries according to explicit rules. Recheck credentials and user intent for ongoing external actions, and provide a clear cancellation mechanism.

192What is a human-in-the-loop checkpoint?Basic

It is a defined pause where a person supplies a decision, correction, or authorization needed for the next step. Save enough state to resume without repeating prior work. 193How do you resume an agent after approval?Intermediate

Verify the approver's authority, match approval to the exact pending action and version, and confirm that material details have not changed. Record the decision and advance the persisted workflow. Represent approval, expiry, cancellation, and execution as competing state transitions governed by atomic checks. 3 topics · 9 questions

Delivery semantics

Basic 1 Q&A

195What does at-least-once delivery mean for agent jobs?Basic

A job can be delivered more than once, especially after worker failures or lost acknowledgements. Consumers must tolerate repeated processing. Use stable job identities and idempotent side effects where possible. A queue's delivery guarantee does not automatically guarantee that an external action occurs only once.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

196What is an idempotency key and where should it be enforced?Intermediate

An idempotency key identifies one intended operation across retries. The service executing the write should atomically bind the key to the request and result, rejecting conflicting reuse. Keep keys stable for retries and distinct for genuinely new actions. Client-side memory alone cannot protect against simultaneous workers or a crash.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

197Why is “exactly once” difficult across an agent and an external API?Advanced

The application cannot generally atomically commit its local state and an unrelated external side effect. A crash between the two can leave an unknown outcome. Use provider-supported idempotency, transactional outbox patterns, reconciliation, and operation status checks as appropriate. State the scope of any exactly-once claim rather than applying it to the entire distributed system.

Failure recovery

Basic 1 Q&A

198What should an agent do when a tool times out?Basic

Treat the result as unknown until the operation's semantics establish otherwise. A read may be safely retried, but a write may already have succeeded. Check operation status or retry using a stable idempotency key. Report uncertainty clearly instead of assuming a timeout means nothing happened.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

199How do circuit breakers protect agent services?Intermediate

A circuit breaker temporarily stops calls to a repeatedly failing dependency, reducing wasted work and allowing recovery. Track failures, open the breaker under a defined rule, and probe cautiously before closing it. Combine it with timeouts, backoff, and a useful degraded path. Do not classify user validation failures as dependency outages.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

200How do compensation actions differ from transaction rollback?Advanced

Rollback can restore uncommitted changes within a transaction's guarantees. Compensation is a new action that attempts to offset an already completed external effect, such as issuing a refund after a charge. It may fail or leave an audit history and cannot always restore the original situation. Design and authorize compensations explicitly.

Concurrency and consistency

Basic 1 Q&A

201Why can parallel agents overwrite each other's work?Basic

Workers can read the same old state and produce competing updates without knowing another change occurred. Shared files and records need ownership or concurrency controls. Partition independent work when possible and merge deliberately. Natural-language instructions to be careful do not prevent a race at the storage layer.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

202When should you use optimistic concurrency for agent state?Intermediate

Use versioned updates when conflicts are possible but uncommon and retries are acceptable. Read a version, compute a change, and commit only if the version still matches; otherwise reload and reconsider. Avoid blindly replaying external actions on conflict. The retry must account for any work already completed.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

203How do you maintain invariants across multiple workers and services?Advanced

Identify the service that owns each invariant, such as a remaining budget or order status, and enforce atomic state changes there. Use transactions for local invariants and explicit coordination or reconciliation for cross-service processes. Test partitions, retries, and stale reads. A global model conversation is not a substitute for a consistent accounting boundary.

Unit tests check a narrow implementation contract under controlled inputs. Agent evaluations measure behavior across tasks where model choices may vary. Check valid and invalid arguments, permission enforcement, result shape, known errors, timeouts, side effects, and idempotency where relevant. Keep tests focused on the external contract rather than duplicating internal implementation details.

Use an isolated resettable environment with synthetic or appropriately de-identified data and scoped credentials. Clearly distinguish simulation success from evidence about live-provider behavior.

Real requests omit fields, use conflicting terminology, or ask for unavailable capabilities. It checks an expected relationship between outputs after a controlled input change. For example, reordering irrelevant documents should not change a supported conclusion, while changing an authorized spending limit should change eligible actions. Use domain-valid transformations and explicit expectations. Such tests reveal brittleness without requiring one exact text answer.

Maintain benign lookalike cases so a defense is not rewarded simply for refusing every task.

Versioning preserves the exact cases, environments, and grading rules behind a reported result. Otherwise an apparent improvement may come from an easier dataset or changed labels. Capture the smallest realistic case that reproduces the failure, then add nearby cases that distinguish the root cause from unrelated behavior. Include the protected outcome and expected recovery. Prioritize explicit product requirements and risk thresholds, then inspect task slices, sample sizes, and grading reliability. Avoid collapsing every dimension into one opaque average score.

Capture the run and operation IDs, tool version, validated argument metadata, authorization result, start and end times, status, retry count, and provider request ID where available. Include tracing vendors and exports in the data-governance model rather than treating logs as harmless metadata.

An SLO defines a measurable target for a user-relevant outcome over a period, such as a specified share of supported tasks completing within a latency and correctness threshold. Compare against release versions and control groups where feasible. Watch for changes in user mix and source data. A decrease in complaints alone may reflect lower usage rather than improved quality.

Basic 1 Q&A

219What should an operator do first during an agent incident?Basic

Contain the affected capability, preserve relevant evidence, assess user impact, and identify whether external side effects continue. Use scoped controls such as disabling a tool or reverting a configuration rather than deleting evidence. Communicate confirmed facts and unknowns. Restoration should include checking task state, not only restarting workers.

Intermediate 1 Q&A

220How do you investigate an unintended external action?Intermediate

Correlate the user request, authorization policy, model proposal, actual executed arguments, and downstream result. Determine whether the cause was ambiguous intent, permission failure, injection, retry duplication, or a tool defect. Reconcile affected state and contact appropriate owners through authorized channels. Build the fix around the execution boundary that failed.

221What makes an agent postmortem actionable?Advanced

Document impact, timeline, contributing technical and organizational factors, containment, and the evidence supporting the root-cause analysis. Assign concrete improvements with owners and verification criteria. Include why existing tests or controls did not detect the issue. Avoid attributing everything to the model when tool design, permissions, or recovery behavior amplified the failure.

Identity, authorization and secrets

3 topics · 9 questions

Identity boundaries

Basic 1 Q&A

222How are authentication and authorization different?Basic

Authentication establishes who is making a request; authorization determines what that identity may do to a resource. An agent may act on behalf of a user, but its tool calls still require resource-level checks. A logged-in session alone is not permission to read every record or perform every action.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

223What is a confused-deputy problem in an agent system?Intermediate

A more privileged component may be induced to use its authority on behalf of a less privileged requester. An agent with broad service credentials can become that deputy if tool requests are not bound to the real user's permissions. Enforce the caller's scope at the owning service and avoid allowing prompt text to select a more privileged identity.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

224How do you design delegated authorization for long-running agents?Advanced

Bind each run to a verified principal and explicit delegated scope, with expiry, revocation, and auditability. Recheck authority before consequential operations, especially after long waits or membership changes. Use short-lived credentials or brokered access where appropriate. A permission granted when a run started may no longer be valid when it resumes.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Credential handling

Basic 1 Q&A

225Why should secrets stay out of agent prompts?Basic

Prompts can be logged, forwarded, included in traces, or exposed through injection and accidental output. Give tools access to credentials through a controlled runtime or secret broker instead. The model typically needs to know a capability exists, not the underlying token. Redaction reduces exposure but does not replace least privilege.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

226How do you scope credentials for individual tools?Intermediate

Grant only required operations and resources, separate reads from writes where practical, and bind access to the correct tenant and user context. Use distinct credentials or scoped tokens rather than a global administrator key. Rotate and revoke them through managed mechanisms. Validate that the downstream service actually enforces the requested scope.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

227What should happen when a credential is revoked during a run?Advanced

Stop new operations that depend on that credential, record the blocked state, and avoid retries that silently substitute a more privileged identity. Determine whether already submitted external actions completed. Resume only with valid authorization according to the task's rules. Preserve enough state for a clear user explanation and safe continuation.

Access-policy enforcement

Basic 1 Q&A

228Where should an agent's permissions be enforced?Basic

Enforce permissions in the runtime and the service that owns the resource, before the operation occurs. Prompts can explain policy but cannot act as the only gate. Validate both operation type and resource scope. A tool that accepts arbitrary tenant IDs must not trust the model to choose only authorized ones.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

229What is the difference between RBAC and ABAC for agent tools?Intermediate

Role-based access control grants permissions through roles. Attribute-based access control uses attributes such as user, resource, tenant, time, or workflow state. Systems often combine them. Choose a policy that can express the required constraints and explain decisions. The model can supply task context, but trusted services must determine authoritative attributes.

Advanced 1 Q&A

230How do you test that an agent cannot cross tenant boundaries?Advanced

Create adversarial cases with similar record names, guessed IDs, shared indexes, cached results, and changing memberships. Check retrieval, tools, exports, traces, and memory, not just the UI. Verify denial occurs before sensitive data reaches the model. Use automated policy tests plus end-to-end runs under realistic identities.

231What is an agent skill or instruction package?Basic

It is a reusable set of task-specific guidance, examples, scripts, or references that an agent can load when relevant. Formats differ across products. Use trusted distribution, review executable content and external destinations, pin versions where appropriate, and audit updates. It lets the agent obtain relevant tool descriptions without placing every integration in every request. This can reduce context and selection ambiguity. Measure whether the necessary tools are retrieved, whether irrelevant or forbidden tools appear, and whether the agent chooses and calls the right contract. Identify the applicable scope and established precedence, compare the conflicting requirements, and use current task authorization where it resolves the issue. 3 topics · 9 questions

Feedback signals

Basic 1 Q&A

240What kinds of feedback can improve an agent system?Basic

Useful signals include verified task outcomes, user corrections, tool errors, expert labels, and well-designed preference comparisons. Each has bias: user satisfaction may reward confidence, and tool success may not mean the user's goal was met. Record provenance and evaluate before using feedback to change behavior.

Intermediate 1 Q&A

241How do you turn production failures into useful learning data?Intermediate

Identify the root cause, reconstruct the necessary context, remove sensitive data, and label the correct action or outcome. Include nearby counterexamples so a fix generalizes. Separate tool defects and authorization failures from model behavior that training could change. Keep a held-out evaluation set that is not recycled into tuning.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

242How do you prevent feedback loops from reinforcing bad behavior?Advanced

Audit who supplies feedback, what it rewards, and whether the signal correlates with real task success. Track distribution shifts and adversarial manipulation. Require independent evaluation before promoting changes, especially from self-generated labels. A system that judges and trains only on its own confident outputs can amplify errors.

Reinforcement learning concepts

Basic 1 Q&A

243What is reinforcement learning in the context of agents?Basic

Reinforcement learning optimizes a policy using feedback about actions and outcomes in an environment. An LLM-based agent may be trained with task rewards or preference-derived signals, but many deployed agents do not learn online at all. Distinguish training the model from changing prompts, memory, or routing during application operation.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

244What is reward hacking?Intermediate

Reward hacking occurs when a policy improves the measured reward without meeting the intended objective. For example, an agent might close support tickets quickly while leaving customers unresolved. Use outcome checks, adversarial cases, and multiple measures that expose shortcuts. A more detailed reward is not automatically safe if it still omits important behavior.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

245How would you evaluate a policy optimized for multi-step tool use?Advanced

Use environments with independently checked outcomes, explicit action constraints, and held-out tasks that differ from training. Measure total success, unsafe actions, cost, and recovery, not just per-call accuracy. Test whether reward-improving shortcuts exploit simulator artifacts. Assess generalization to realistic tool failures before allowing broader deployment.

Continuous improvement

Basic 1 Q&A

246Can an agent improve without changing model weights?Basic

Yes. Better tool contracts, retrieval, instructions, memory selection, validation, and workflow design can improve task success. These changes alter the environment and information available to the model. Measure them with controlled comparisons. Calling the improvement learning should not obscure whether the model itself was actually updated.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

247How do you prioritize agent improvements?Intermediate

Group failures by frequency, impact, and root cause, then estimate the expected benefit and effort of each change. Fix deterministic defects and broken permissions before adding more reasoning loops. Use a representative baseline and a small experiment to validate the intervention. Track cost per successful task as well as accuracy.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

248How do you govern automatic prompt or policy optimization?Advanced

Limit the search space, use approved training data, and evaluate candidates against held-out quality and policy criteria. Version every candidate and require appropriate review before production promotion. Keep rollback available and prevent optimizers from modifying their own evaluation controls. Improvement in one metric is insufficient evidence for unrestricted self-modification.

249What should a coding agent inspect before changing a repository?Basic

Read applicable project instructions, locate the relevant implementation, and understand the current behavior and local conventions. Inspect the working tree so existing user changes are preserved. State the observed problem, expected behavior, scope, constraints, and acceptance evidence. Include a concrete failing scenario or reproduction when available. Inspect current changes, give one owner to each overlapping file or region, and coordinate integration explicitly. Avoid resetting or overwriting work the agent did not create. 252Why is a compiling program not enough evidence of a successful agent change?Basic

Compilation checks syntax and some type constraints, but the feature can still violate requirements, break a user flow, or mishandle data. Verify behavior appropriate to the change and inspect the diff. For visible interfaces, review the rendered result. Report any verification limits clearly.

Select checks that cover the changed behavior and likely regressions, following applicable project requirements. Avoid writing trivial tests that simply repeat the implementation without checking a useful contract.

Use representative tasks with hidden acceptance checks, realistic repository state, and constraints on unrelated changes. Prevent evaluation leakage from issue answers or reference patches where possible.

Keep the final scope coherent, inspect the diff, complete relevant checks, and write a description around the concrete problem and resulting behavior. Include validation and meaningful risks. Check the underlying primary evidence rather than citing one article that repeats another unsupported claim. Track whether a source reports firsthand findings or summarizes someone else. Define a rubric for coverage, source authority, factual support, uncertainty handling, and usefulness for the user's decision. Use expert review and calibrated automated checks where appropriate. Use code for reproducible calculations, data transformations, statistical analysis, and plots when the task benefits from exact execution. Inspect the data schema and units first. Distinguish descriptive patterns, predictive associations, and causal effects. Separate source-supported facts from stylistic choices and original inference. Keep evidence references for factual claims and flag missing information rather than inventing it. Review names, numbers, quotations, and dates carefully. A polished sentence can still be factually wrong.

Intermediate 1 Q&A

298How do you handle fairness between heavy and light users?Intermediate

Apply tenant or user quotas, weighted scheduling where appropriate, and concurrency limits that prevent long runs from monopolizing capacity. Make admission and cancellation behavior predictable. Measure waiting time by user segment. Fairness policy should reflect the product's commitments rather than emerge accidentally from queue ordering.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

299How do you plan for cascading overload in a multi-step agent platform?Advanced

Model how retries and fan-out amplify demand across providers and tools. Use backpressure, bounded queues, deadlines, per-dependency concurrency limits, and load shedding. Test partial outages and recovery rather than only steady-state throughput. A degraded dependency should not trigger unlimited parallel retries that exhaust the rest of the platform.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Product fit

Basic 1 Q&A

300How do you decide whether a task should become an agent feature?Basic

Identify a recurring user problem, the required access, a measurable outcome, and why a simpler interface or workflow is insufficient. Estimate operational cost and consequences of failure. Validate with real users and a bounded prototype. Agent autonomy is a design choice, not a product benefit by itself.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

301How do you measure an agent's value to users?Intermediate

Measure task completion, saved effort, quality, trust, and user control using appropriate baselines and research methods. Track abandonment and corrections alongside adoption. Distinguish novelty-driven use from sustained utility. A feature can generate many interactions while creating more review work than it saves.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

302When should you reduce an agent's scope after launch?Advanced

Reduce scope when evidence shows repeated failures, unacceptable intervention cost, poor economics, or risk outside the supported operating conditions. Identify which task slices still provide value and constrain access accordingly. Communicate supported behavior clearly and evaluate the narrower system. Fewer capabilities can produce a more dependable product.

CATEGORY 33 / 34

Open standards and agent interoperability

3 topics · 9 questions

Protocol boundaries

Basic 1 Q&A

303How is agent-to-agent communication different from tool calling?Basic

Tool calling usually requests a defined operation from a capability. Agent-to-agent communication can delegate a broader task with progress, negotiation, or artifacts. Boundaries vary by implementation. In both cases, define identity, permissions, schemas, timeouts, and completion criteria rather than relying on informal conversation alone.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

304What should an inter-agent task contract contain?Intermediate

Include the goal, authorized scope, inputs, expected outputs, deadlines, budget, status model, artifact format, and cancellation behavior. Specify which party owns external side effects and how failures are reported. Avoid assuming both agents share hidden conversation context. Explicit contracts make integration and evaluation possible.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

305How do you establish trust between independently operated agents?Advanced

Authenticate services, verify the delegating identity and permitted scope, validate artifacts, and enforce policy at every receiving boundary. Limit transitive delegation and audit consequential actions. A protocol handshake proves compatibility or identity only within its guarantees; it does not establish that another agent's reasoning or evidence is correct.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Artifacts and schemas

Basic 1 Q&A

306Why should agents exchange structured artifacts?Basic

Structured artifacts define fields and status explicitly, reducing ambiguity in handoffs and allowing validation. Examples include a research evidence bundle or a code-change report. Preserve references to original sources and distinguish unknown from absent data. Human-readable summaries remain useful but should not be the only machine contract for important workflows.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

307How do you evolve schemas used by multiple agents?Intermediate

Use version identifiers, backward-compatible additions where feasible, and explicit migrations for breaking changes. Define required fields and unknown-field behavior. Validate both producers and consumers with shared contract tests. Do not silently change the meaning of an existing field while retaining its name.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

308How do you preserve provenance across a chain of delegations?Advanced

Carry stable task, source, and artifact identifiers with timestamps, authorship or service identity, and transformations performed. Preserve links to supporting evidence and permission scope. Validate provenance claims where they affect trust. A final summary should not erase which parts were observed, inferred, or supplied by an untrusted participant.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Interoperability operations

Basic 1 Q&A

309What is capability negotiation between agent systems?Basic

It is a process for discovering which features, versions, and operations each participant supports. Use the negotiated result to select compatible behavior and reject unsupported requests clearly. Discovery should be permission-scoped. Advertising a capability does not mean every caller is authorized to use it.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

310How do you handle cancellation across delegated agents?Intermediate

Define a cancellation identifier and state transition, propagate the request to active workers, and report which operations stopped versus already completed. Use deadlines and cleanup rules for abandoned work. Cancellation is best-effort for external actions already accepted by another service, so reconcile results rather than promising universal rollback.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

311How do you test interoperability without assuming one vendor's behavior?Advanced

Build protocol conformance and contract tests covering schemas, version negotiation, errors, timeouts, retries, cancellation, and permission denial. Run against multiple independent implementations when possible. Include malformed and unexpected inputs. Successful message exchange is only the first step; verify end-to-end task state and protected boundaries.

Advanced architecture and frontier concepts

3 topics · 9 questions

World models and simulation

Basic 1 Q&A

312What is a world model in an agent discussion?Basic

The term often refers to a representation that predicts aspects of an environment and how actions may change it. It may be learned or explicitly coded, and usage varies across research and products. Distinguish a model's plausible imagined outcome from an observed external result. Define the term before making capability claims.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

313How can simulation help an agent choose actions?Intermediate

A simulator can estimate candidate outcomes under specified assumptions, helping compare plans before execution. Validate how well it represents the real task and account for uncertainty. Keep simulated actions separate from real operations. A plan that succeeds in an inaccurate simulator may fail systematically in deployment.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

314How do you prevent an agent from exploiting simulator weaknesses?Advanced

Use held-out environments, varied dynamics, independent outcome checks, and tests outside the optimization simulator. Inspect suspicious shortcuts and compare predicted with observed real-world behavior. Limit deployment based on evidence about transfer. High simulation reward alone is insufficient for a claim of general real-world competence.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Search and deliberation

Basic 1 Q&A

315What is planning search in an agent system?Basic

Planning search explores alternative action sequences or candidate solutions before choosing one. It can be implemented with code, model calls, or both. Search is useful only if candidates can be evaluated meaningfully. Bound compute and compare against a simpler direct approach.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

316When can extra deliberation make an agent worse?Intermediate

It can add latency, cost, contradictory assumptions, and opportunities to overfit a flawed evaluator. A correct simple answer may be revised into an incorrect elaborate one. Use stopping criteria and evidence-based evaluation. More tokens or critique rounds should earn their place through measured task improvements.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

317How do you compare search-based planning with reactive agent loops?Advanced

Evaluate both on tasks with varying horizon, observability, and recovery cost, under comparable total budgets. Measure successful outcomes, constraint violations, compute, and adaptation to unexpected events. Search may help when future consequences can be modeled; reactive loops may suit rapidly changing conditions. Avoid declaring one architecture universally superior.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Self-modification and scope

Basic 1 Q&A

318What is the difference between self-reflection and self-modification?Basic

Self-reflection produces feedback or revised output within a run. Self-modification changes persistent instructions, code, tools, or model parameters. The latter can affect future tasks and needs explicit controls. A generated suggestion to improve a system is not evidence that a safe improvement was applied.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Intermediate 1 Q&A

319How should an agent propose changes to its own tools?Intermediate

Produce a reviewable patch or specification, explain the observed problem, and include validation evidence. Test changes in an isolated environment before promotion. Preserve permission boundaries and version compatibility. The agent proposing a change should not automatically gain authority to weaken the controls that evaluate or authorize it.

Added question · Original answerLink to answer ↗

Advanced 1 Q&A

320How do you evaluate claims of general-purpose autonomous agents?Advanced

Ask for a defined task distribution, operating constraints, failure reporting, intervention rates, and independent outcome checks. Examine contamination, hidden human assistance, and selection of demonstrations. Compare against baselines under equal budgets. Broad marketing language does not establish reliable performance across unseen tasks and environments.
